## **7\. Campaigns (outbound calling at scale)**

| Method & path | What it does |
| ----- | ----- |
| `POST /campaigns` | Create: name, audience filter (e.g., `state=lead, region=GJ`), calling window, pacing (calls/hour), start/end dates |
| `POST /campaigns/{id}/preview` | Shows who would be called — count \+ sample, **after** removing DNC and rule-blocked customers — before anything dials |
| `POST /campaigns/{id}/start` · `/pause` · `/stop` | Control |
| `GET /campaigns/{id}` | Live stats: queued, calling, connected, converted, failed |
| `GET /campaigns/{id}/targets` | Per-customer status inside the campaign, incl. exclusion reasons |

Every single dial still passes the pre-call rule check individually at dial time — a campaign cannot bypass DNC or calling hours even if it was created before a customer opted out.

---

## **8\. Support & Escalations**

| Method & path | What it does |
| ----- | ----- |
| `POST /tickets` · `GET /tickets` · `GET /tickets/{id}` · `PATCH /tickets/{id}` | Standard ticket CRUD: category, priority, status, assignment, resolution. (The AI creates tickets through its tool; these endpoints are for humans) |
| `GET /escalations` | The human work queue: everything the AI handed over, with reason and urgency |
| `POST /escalations/{id}/accept` | A human takes it (also delivers the AI-written context briefing) |
| `POST /escalations/{id}/resolve` | Close it — this also unlocks the customer for automated contact again |

---

## **9\. Calls, Callbacks & Telephony**

| Method & path | What it does |
| ----- | ----- |
| `GET /calls` | Call log: filter by customer, status, direction, date |
| `GET /calls/{id}` | Detail: duration, outcome, retry chain, cost |
| `GET /calls/{id}/recording` | Short-lived signed URL to the audio (access is logged) |
| `POST /calls/outbound` | Manually trigger one outbound call to a customer (passes pre-call rules like everything else) |
| `GET /callbacks` · `PATCH /callbacks/{id}` | The "call me later" queue: view, reschedule, cancel |

### **Webhooks (telephony provider → us)**

`POST /webhooks/telephony/{provider}` — Plivo/Exotel/Twilio send call events here (ringing, answered, hangup, recording ready). The provider adapter translates each provider's format into our canonical events. Secured by provider signature verification, not by API key.

---

## **10\. Consent & Do-Not-Contact**

| Method & path | What it does |
| ----- | ----- |
| `GET /customers/{id}/consents` | The consent ledger: what was granted/revoked, when, with what evidence |
| `POST /customers/{id}/consents` | Record a consent event (type: calls / recording / marketing; granted: true/false) |
| `GET /dnc` | The Do-Not-Contact list |
| `POST /dnc` | Add a number (source: customer request / regulator / import) — takes effect immediately, everywhere |
| `DELETE /dnc/{id}` | Remove — admin only, and the removal itself is audit-logged |
| `POST /dnc/import` | Bulk import (e.g., national DNC registry file) |

---

## **11\. Analytics & Audit**

### **Analytics**

| Method & path | What it does |
| ----- | ----- |
| `GET /analytics/overview?from=&to=` | The headline numbers: calls made, connection rate, conversion rate, appointments booked & completed, tickets resolved |
| `GET /analytics/funnel` | Journey funnel: how many customers sit in each stage, and conversion between stages |
| `GET /analytics/agent` | AI quality numbers: tool-choice accuracy, average confidence, escalation rate, average response latency, hallucination flags |
| `GET /analytics/campaigns/{id}` | Per-campaign results |
| `GET /analytics/export?from=&to=&format=csv` | Raw event export |

### **Audit & explainability ("why did it do that?")**

| Method & path | What it does |
| ----- | ----- |
| `GET /audit/traces/{trace_id}` | The complete record of one decision: what the customer said, what memory and knowledge was used, every rule checked and its verdict, what the AI proposed and why, what validation said, confidence, what happened. This is the flight recorder readout |
| `GET /audit/traces?conversation_id=` | All decisions in one conversation, in order |
| `GET /audit/blocked?from=&to=` | Every action that was blocked, and by which rule — the compliance report |
| `GET /audit/events` | Admin activity log: who changed which rule/setting, when, old → new value |

---

## **12\. Everything Else**

**Auth & users:** `POST /auth/login` · `POST /auth/refresh` · `POST /auth/logout` · CRUD on `/users` and `/roles` · CRUD on `/api-keys` (admin).

**Async jobs:** long tasks (imports, document processing) return `{ "job_id": ... }` immediately. Check progress: `GET /jobs/{id}` → `{ status: "processing" | "done" | "failed", progress: 0.7, result: ... }`.

**Health:** `GET /health` (is the API up) · `GET /health/deep` (DB, Redis, providers — for monitoring).

### **Live updates (WebSocket)**

`WS /ws/dashboard` — the dashboard subscribes and receives pushed events, so screens update without refreshing:

| Event | When |
| ----- | ----- |
| `call.started` / `call.ended` | Live call monitor |
| `call.turn` | A live call's latest exchange (for the "listen in" view) |
| `escalation.created` | A human is needed — this is the alert that matters |
| `appointment.booked` | Bookings ticker |
| `campaign.progress` | Campaign counters |

---

## **13\. One Worked Example (tying it together)**

A typical outbound sales call touches the API like this:

1. Campaign worker: pre-call rules pass → tells telephony to dial  
2. Provider → `POST /webhooks/telephony/plivo` (call answered)  
3. Voice service → `POST /conversations` (start, direction: outbound)  
4. Voice service → `POST /conversations/{id}/turns` — repeated for every exchange; one of these turns internally books the appointment via the booking tool  
5. Voice service → `POST /conversations/{id}/end` — triggers summary \+ memory update in the background  
6. Dashboard (already connected to `WS /ws/dashboard`) shows `appointment.booked` in real time  
7. A supervisor later opens `GET /audit/traces?conversation_id=...` and reads exactly why the AI offered Saturday instead of Friday

# Voice Pipeline Design

# **Voice Pipeline Design**

---

## **1\. What This Document Covers**

Everything between the telephone network and the brain:

* How a phone call reaches our system (and how we place calls)  
* How the customer's speech becomes text, and our text becomes speech  
* The **one-second problem** — why voice is hard, and our plan to keep replies fast  
* Handling real conversation behavior: interruptions, silences, background noise  
* Recording, disclosures, transfers to humans, and what happens when things break

This is the domain of the **Voice Session Service** — the separate service from the architecture doc. One instance of it handles many simultaneous calls; each call lives inside a "session" object that owns everything about that call.

---

## **2\. The Cast of Characters**

**Telephony provider (Plivo / Exotel / Twilio).** The company that connects us to the actual phone network. They give us phone numbers, place and receive calls for us, and — critically — give us a **live audio stream** of the call over a WebSocket, in both directions. We hear the caller through it, and whatever audio we push into it, the caller hears.

**STT — Speech-to-Text (Deepgram, Azure fallback).** We stream the caller's audio to it continuously, and it streams text back *as the person speaks* — first as rough "partial" guesses, then a "final" version once the sentence is complete. Like live subtitles being typed and corrected in real time.

**TTS — Text-to-Speech (ElevenLabs / Azure Neural).** The reverse: we stream text in, it streams natural-sounding audio out. The important property we need: it starts producing audio within \~200 ms of receiving the first words, rather than waiting for the whole sentence.

**The brain (Core Platform).** Receives the finished text of each customer turn via `process_turn`, returns what to say. Covered fully in the Core Engine doc.

All three external pieces sit behind our provider abstraction layer — each can be swapped or failed-over without touching pipeline logic.

---

## **3\. Life of a Call**

### **Inbound (customer calls us)**

1. Provider receives the call on our number → sends a webhook: "incoming call from \+91-XXXXX."  
2. We look up the caller: `GET /customers/lookup?phone=...`. Known customer → their file is preloaded. Unknown → a new lead record is created on the spot.  
3. We answer and immediately open the media stream (the two-way audio WebSocket).  
4. **The disclosure plays first** — "This call may be recorded..." — from a pre-generated audio file (no TTS delay), and the call record is marked `disclosure_played = true`. Recording starts only after this.  
5. A conversation is opened in the core (`POST /conversations`), and the greeting is spoken. The turn loop (Section 4\) begins.

### **Outbound (we call the customer)**

1. A trigger fires: campaign, retry timer, reminder, or a "call me later" coming due.  
2. The worker asks the core to run **pre-call rule checks** (DNC, calling hours, retry limits, consent). Any block → the call never happens, the reason is logged.  
3. Checks pass → we tell the provider to dial.  
4. The provider reports what happened: **answered** → same as inbound from step 3 onward. **Busy / no answer** → a retry is scheduled per the retry rules. **Voicemail detected** → hang up without speaking (configurable per tenant: some prefer leaving a short message).  
5. One extra politeness step for outbound: the agent confirms it's speaking to the right person before anything else ("Am I speaking with Mr. Sharma?").

### **Ending**

Either side hangs up, or the brain returns `end_call: true` (conversation concluded politely). We close the media stream, tell the core (`POST /conversations/{id}/end`), and the post-call pipeline (summary, fact extraction, memory update) runs in the background. The recording is uploaded to storage and linked to the call record.

---

## **4\. The Turn Loop — the Heart of the Pipeline**

A "turn" \= the customer says something, we reply. Here is what actually happens inside one turn:

**1\. Listening.** Caller's audio flows continuously: provider → us → STT. STT sends back partial transcripts ("I want", "I want to book", "I want to book an appointment").

**2\. Knowing when they've finished.** This is trickier than it sounds — humans pause mid-sentence. We combine three signals: the STT's own "final transcript" marker, a silence detector (VAD — voice activity detection) watching the audio energy, and a minimum-silence timer (\~600–800 ms, tunable). Only when the signals agree do we declare: turn complete.

**3\. Thinking.** The final text goes to the brain: `POST /conversations/{id}/turns`. While the brain thinks, the caller hears silence — this is the window we fight to keep short (Section 5).

**4\. Speaking.** The brain's reply comes back split into sentences (`response_segments`). We push sentence 1 into TTS immediately and start playing its audio while sentences 2 and 3 are still being synthesized. The caller starts hearing the answer as early as possible.

**5\. Back to listening.** The moment we finish speaking (or get interrupted — Section 6), we're listening again.

The session object tracks which phase the call is in at every moment: `listening → thinking → speaking → listening...`. Every phase change is timestamped, which is how we measure latency per turn in production.

---

## **5\. The One-Second Problem**

In human conversation, a reply that takes longer than \~1.5 seconds feels broken — people say "hello? are you there?". This is the single hardest engineering constraint in the project.

![][image4]

Our budget per turn (from the customer's last word to the first sound of our reply):

| Stage | Budget | Notes |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Detecting they've finished speaking | \~250 ms | The silence timer is most of this — it's a *deliberate* wait, tunable |
| Final transcript from STT | \~100 ms | Deepgram streaming is fast; this is mostly network |
| The brain (`process_turn`) | \~650 ms | Understand \+ decide \+ act \+ compose (2–3 LLM calls) |
| First audio byte from TTS | \~200 ms | Streaming TTS, first sentence only |
| **Total** | **\~1.2 s** | Acceptable. Anything over \~2 s needs the tricks below |

**The tricks that keep us under budget:**

1. **Stream everything.** Never wait for a full anything — partial transcripts flow while the customer talks; TTS starts on sentence 1 while the brain may still be finalizing sentence 3\.  
2. **Start thinking early (speculative start).** When the partial transcript has been stable for a moment and VAD says the voice has stopped, we send the turn to the brain *before* the full silence timer expires. If the customer resumes talking, we throw the speculative result away. Saves 300–500 ms on most turns.  
3. **Acknowledgment fillers.** For turns we know will be slow (a tool doing real work — booking, searching), the brain flags it, and the voice layer immediately plays a short natural filler — "Sure, one moment…" — from pre-generated audio, while the real work happens behind it. The perceived wait drops to near zero.  
4. **Fast model for understanding.** Step 2 of the planner uses a small, fast model; the big model is reserved for deciding and composing.  
5. **Pre-generated audio for fixed phrases.** Disclosure, greetings, fillers, "goodbye" — all cached audio files per tenant persona. Zero synthesis time.  
6. **Region matters.** The voice service is deployed in the same Azure region as the telephony provider's India endpoints; STT/TTS providers chosen with India POPs. Every 100 ms of round-trip matters when you cross it 3 times per turn.

**Measurement is built in:** every turn records per-stage timings into the decision trace. The dashboard's agent analytics show p50/p95 latency per stage — so when the number creeps up, we know exactly which stage to blame.

---

## **6\. Interruptions (Barge-In)**

Real customers interrupt: we're mid-pitch and they say "actually, how much does it cost?"

What must happen — instantly:

1. VAD detects the caller's voice while we are in the `speaking` phase.  
2. We stop our audio playback **immediately** (target: within \~150 ms — anything slower feels like the agent is talking over them).  
3. Whatever remained unspoken of our reply is discarded, but we note *what was actually said out loud* versus what wasn't — the brain needs to know the customer never heard sentence 3\.  
4. We switch to `listening` and process their interruption as a normal new turn. The note about the unfinished reply goes into the turn metadata so the brain has honest context.

One guard: brief noises (a cough, "hmm", background TV) shouldn't kill our sentence. The interruption only triggers if the detected speech lasts longer than a threshold (\~300 ms of sustained voice) or STT immediately produces words. Below that, we keep talking.

---

## **7\. Silence and Awkward Moments**

**Customer goes quiet mid-call.** After \~6 seconds of silence in the `listening` phase: a gentle prompt ("Are you still there?"). After a second timeout: "Seems like this isn't a good time — I'll call you back later. Have a great day," → polite hangup → the brain records it and schedules a callback per rules. Never an abrupt dead-line hangup.

**Customer speaks but STT produces garbage** (heavy noise, bad line). The STT confidence score arrives with every transcript. Below a threshold, the pipeline doesn't bother the brain — it asks directly: "Sorry, I couldn't hear that clearly — could you repeat?" Two failures in a row → the brain is told, and it typically offers a callback on a better line.

**Both talk at once** (cross-talk). Barge-in rules win: customer speaking always takes priority; we stop.

**DTMF (keypad presses).** Detected by the provider and forwarded to us as events — supported for things like "press 1 to confirm" as an accessibility fallback, though the primary interface is always natural speech.

---

## **8\. Recording, Disclosure & Privacy in the Pipeline**

* Disclosure **always** plays before recording starts and before any conversation happens. It's a hard sequence in the session state machine, not a convention — the code cannot reach `listening` without passing `disclosure_played`.  
* Recordings upload to object storage encrypted, linked to the call record; access is only via the short-lived signed URLs from the API, and every access is logged.  
* Live transcripts flowing through the system are PII-masked before they land in any log file (masking design is in the Compliance doc). The database stores the true transcript; *logs* never do.  
* If the tenant's policy or the customer's region forbids recording, the session runs with recording disabled — the pipeline works identically, just without the tap.

---

## **9\. Transfers to Humans (Warm Transfer)**

When the brain returns `escalation: { type: "immediate" }`:

1. The agent tells the customer honestly: "Let me connect you with my colleague who can help you better. One moment."  
2. Comfort audio (soft hold music / "connecting you now") plays.  
3. Via the provider's API, we dial the human agent's number/extension and bridge the two call legs.  
4. Simultaneously, the human's dashboard pops the **briefing**: who the customer is, journey stage, what happened this call, what's pending — generated by the brain at escalation time.  
5. If no human answers within N seconds (configurable), fallback per rules: "All our team members are busy — I've scheduled a callback for you at 4 PM today." The escalation record stays open either way.  
6. Once bridged, our AI leg goes silent and drops off; recording continues per policy.

---

## **10\. When Components Fail Mid-Call**

| Failure | What the caller experiences | What actually happens |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| STT provider goes down | A brief "sorry, could you repeat that?" | Circuit breaker flips to the fallback STT within one turn; ops alert fires |
| TTS provider goes down | Slightly different voice mid-call | Same — fallback TTS takes over; better a voice change than silence |
| The brain times out (\>3 s) | "Give me just a second…" then a real answer, or a graceful exit | One retry; if still failing: apology \+ "I'll call you right back" \+ automatic callback \+ alert |
| Voice service instance crashes | Call drops | Provider webhook tells us the call died; the conversation is closed as `abandoned`; post-call pipeline still runs on whatever transcript exists; customer gets a callback |
| Media WebSocket hiccups | A moment of silence | Auto-reconnect with jitter buffer; sessions tolerate \~2 s of stream gap |

The principle everywhere: **never leave the customer in dead air without an explanation, and never lose the record of what happened.**

---

## **11\. Scaling & Deployment Notes**

* One voice service process comfortably handles **\~50–80 concurrent calls** (it's I/O-bound — mostly shuffling audio bytes); we scale horizontally by adding instances behind the load balancer. Calls are sticky to their instance (the session lives in process memory, backed by Redis snapshots for crash recovery).  
* Audio format on the wire is 8 kHz μ-law (telephone standard) — we transcode to/from 16 kHz PCM for STT/TTS at the edge of the service.  
* Concurrency limits per tenant (max simultaneous calls) are enforced here, feeding back into campaign pacing.  
* Load testing before launch: synthetic calls with recorded audio at 2× expected peak, measuring the per-stage latency distributions — the pass criterion is p95 under 2 s end-to-end.

# Compliance, Security & Audit Design

# **Compliance, Security & Audit Design**

---

## **1\. What This Document Covers**

An AI that autonomously calls people and handles their personal data must be provably trustworthy — not "we believe it behaves," but "here is the record showing it behaved." This document covers the five pillars of that:

1. **Consent & Do-Not-Contact** — never contacting anyone we shouldn't  
2. **Recording & disclosure** — doing the legally required things on every call  
3. **Personal data protection (PII)** — who can see what, and how data is guarded  
4. **Access control (RBAC)** — humans and the AI both operate on least privilege  
5. **The audit trail** — every decision explainable after the fact

A theme you'll notice throughout: wherever possible, compliance is **enforced by structure** (the code physically cannot do the wrong thing) rather than by policy (the code is asked nicely). Structural guarantees are called out explicitly below.

---

## **2\. Consent Management**

### **What we track**

Consent is not one yes/no — we track it per purpose, in an **append-only ledger** (`consent_records`). Nothing is ever edited or deleted; a change of mind is a *new entry*:

| Consent type | Covers |
| ----- | ----- |
| `calls` | May we call this person at all |
| `recording` | May we record the call |
| `marketing` | May we make promotional/sales calls (vs. only service calls like reminders) |
| `data_processing` | May we store and process their information |

Each entry stores: granted or revoked, when, through which channel, and **evidence** — for verbal consent, a pointer to the exact clip in the call recording where they said yes. If a regulator ever asks "prove this person consented," the answer is a database row pointing at audio.

### **How consent is captured**

* **Imported leads** carry consent metadata from the source (the client asserts it; we record the assertion and its origin).  
* **During calls**, the agent can ask for consent when needed, and a high-confidence "yes" writes a ledger entry referencing that moment in the recording.  
* **Revocation is instant and structural:** "stop calling me" triggers the DNC signal (below), which no rule, campaign, or human enthusiasm can override.

---

## **3\. Do-Not-Contact (DNC)**

The single most important compliance behavior: **a person who opted out is never contacted again.**

### **Enforcement points — four layers deep**

1. **At dial time (structural).** Every outbound call — campaign, retry, reminder, callback, or manually triggered — passes the pre-call rule check, and the DNC rule is `priority: 0, terminal: true`: it runs first, and if it matches, evaluation stops. There is no code path to the dialer that skips this check.  
2. **At campaign creation.** The audience preview already excludes DNC numbers, so the humans planning a campaign see the truth.  
3. **In-call.** If a customer says "don't call me again," the DNC signal fires: the customer's stage moves to `do_not_contact` (a terminal stage — no transitions out except by an admin with a logged reason), their number goes on the DNC list *immediately, mid-call*, and the agent confirms it to them: "Understood — I've removed you from our calling list. You won't hear from us again."  
4. **On the state machine itself.** The `do_not_contact` transition is the only transition defined with **no guard** — no rule can block it, no confidence threshold applies. Opting out always works.

### **The list itself**

* Scoped entries: `all` (nothing ever) vs. `marketing` (promotional blocked, but service calls like "your appointment is tomorrow" allowed — a distinction Indian telecom rules recognize).  
* Sources tracked: customer request, regulator list import (e.g., national DNC registry), manual entry.  
* Matching is on the normalized phone number — a customer with two records still can't be called on that number.  
* **Removal from the list is admin-only**, requires a typed reason, and is itself an audit event. Additions are one click; removals are deliberately heavy.

---

## **4\. Recording & Disclosure**

* The disclosure ("this call may be recorded…") plays **before** recording starts and before any conversation — enforced by the voice session's internal state machine, which cannot reach the listening phase without passing through `disclosure_played` (structural). The flag is stored on every call record.  
* Per-tenant and per-region configuration: disclosure text, whether recording is on at all, and retention period. A tenant operating where recording requires explicit verbal consent can enable a consent-question flow before recording begins.  
* Recordings are encrypted in storage, playable only through short-lived signed URLs issued by the API, and **every playback is logged** — who listened to which call, when.

---

## **5\. Protecting Personal Data (PII)**

### **The three places data lives, and the rule for each**

| Where | Rule |
| ----- | ----- |
| **The database** | The true data lives here — encrypted at rest (disk-level \+ Postgres), reachable only through the API with role checks. This is the one place real PII is allowed to be. |
| **Log files** | **Never contain raw PII (structural).** All logging goes through one wrapper that masks before writing: phone numbers become `+91-98XXXXXX21`, emails `r***l@adv***.com`, and transcripts are logged only as IDs, never as text. Developers cannot accidentally log a phone number, because the logger won't let them. |
| **LLM providers** | Prompts are built from context blocks, and the builder masks direct identifiers that the model doesn't need: the model sees "the customer" and their preferences, not their phone number or email. What the model genuinely needs to converse (first name, city, product interests) is sent under our data-processing agreements with the providers. Providers are configured for zero data retention where offered. |

### **Additional measures**

* **Encryption in transit** everywhere: TLS on every external and internal hop, including the media WebSockets.  
* **Field-level encryption** for the most sensitive columns (beyond disk encryption), keys in Azure Key Vault, rotated on schedule.  
* **Data retention:** per-tenant policy — recordings kept N months, transcripts M months, then automatically purged by a scheduled job that logs what it deleted. Aligned with India's DPDP Act principle of not keeping data longer than needed.  
* **Right to erasure:** a customer deletion request runs a documented pipeline: personal fields anonymized, recordings deleted, facts purged — while the anonymized interaction skeleton (needed for aggregate analytics and legal defense) is retained. The deletion itself is an audit event.

---

## **6\. Access Control (RBAC)**

### **Human roles**

| Role | Can | Cannot |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| `agent` | View customers, calls, appointments; handle escalations; create tickets | Change rules, tools, or configuration; export data; hear recordings by default |
| `supervisor` | Everything agents can \+ listen to recordings, correct AI memory facts, manually move customer stages, manage escalation queue | Change engine configuration; manage users |
| `admin` | Everything: rules, tools, prompts, packs, users, DNC removals, API keys | — (but every admin action is logged, see §7) |
| `analyst` | Read-only analytics and audit views | See raw PII (their views get masked fields), change anything |

Permissions are granular strings (`customers:read`, `rules:write`, `recordings:listen`…) grouped into these roles; custom roles are possible per tenant. Every API endpoint declares its required permission — the check is in one middleware, not scattered through handlers.

### **The AI's own permissions**

The AI is also a permission-holding actor, deliberately *less* privileged than an admin:

* Each tool declares its `permission_level` — most are `agent`\-level; destructive or bulk operations can be marked `supervisor_only` or `human_only`, making them **invisible to the AI entirely** (they never enter the candidate list — structural).  
* The AI cannot: delete customers, remove DNC entries, edit rules or its own prompts, access other tenants, or export data. Not "instructed not to" — there is no tool for it.

### **API keys**

Service keys are scoped ("this key can read customers and post turns, nothing else"), expire, and are shown once at creation (only a hash is stored). Per-key rate limits.

---

## **7\. The Audit Trail**

Two complementary records answer two different questions:

### **"Why did the AI do that?" — decision traces**

Every conversational turn writes one `decision_traces` row containing the complete picture: what the customer said, which memory entries and knowledge chunks were consulted (by ID — reproducible), every rule evaluated and its verdict, the AI's proposed action and stated reasoning, validation outcomes, the confidence score and band, what was ultimately done, which prompt versions and model produced it, and per-stage latency.

This makes the PRD's explainability requirements literal one-query lookups:

| Question | Answer source |
| ----- | ----- |
| Why was this tool selected? | `planner_reasoning` \+ the candidate list in the trace |
| Why was an action blocked? | `rules_evaluated` — the exact rule, with its reason string |
| Which memories influenced this? | `retrieved_memory` — fact IDs consulted that turn |
| Which knowledge was used? | `retrieved_chunks` — chunk IDs \+ relevance scores |
| Would this happen again? | Re-run with the same prompt versions (hashed in the trace) |

The dashboard renders a trace as a readable timeline — a supervisor clicks any turn of any call and reads the full story. No engineer, no log-diving.

### **"Who changed the system?" — admin audit events**

Every configuration change writes an `audit_events` row: actor, action, resource, **before and after values**, IP, timestamp. Covers: rule edits and activations, tool enable/disable, prompt changes, user/role changes, DNC removals, recording access, data exports, manual stage overrides, memory-fact corrections.

Audit rows are append-only — no API exists to edit or delete them (structural). Retention: minimum 3 years or per contract.

### **Standing compliance reports**

Built as saved queries over these two tables: all blocked actions in a period (and by which rule) · all DNC additions/removals · all recording accesses · all escalations with reasons · hallucination-flag incidents. Exportable for a client's compliance team.

---

## **8\. Platform Security Basics**

* **Webhooks** from telephony providers are verified by provider signature (each adapter implements its provider's scheme); unsigned or invalid payloads are rejected and alerted.  
* **Rate limiting** per key/user/IP at the gateway; login endpoints get strict limits \+ lockout with backoff.  
* **Secrets** (provider API keys, DB credentials, signing keys) live in Azure Key Vault, injected at runtime — never in code, images, or environment files in the repo.  
* **Network posture:** only the API gateway and the telephony webhook/media endpoints are public. Database, Redis, and workers are on a private network. SSH by key only, no password auth.  
* **Dependencies** scanned in CI (pip-audit / npm audit); base images pinned and rebuilt on schedule.  
* **Tenant isolation** is enforced twice: every repository query is tenant-filtered (application layer), *and* Postgres row-level security is enabled on the sensitive tables as a second net — a bug in the first layer still hits the second (structural, defense in depth).  
* **Backups:** automated nightly, encrypted, restore-tested monthly (a backup that was never restored is a hope, not a backup).

---

## **9\. Regulatory Mapping (India-first)**

| Requirement | Where it's handled |
| ----- | ----- |
| TRAI/TCCCPR telemarketing rules — DND registry, permitted calling hours (typically 9 AM–9 PM), promotional vs. transactional distinction | DNC list with scopes (§3) \+ `calling_policy` rules; national registry importable via `/dnc/import` |
| Recording disclosure | §4, structural |
| DPDP Act 2023 — consent, purpose limitation, retention limits, erasure rights | Consent ledger (§2), retention jobs \+ deletion pipeline (§5) |
| Sector rules for specific clients (e.g., IRDAI for insurance, RBI adjacency for lending) | Arrive as pack-level rule sets and disclosure scripts — the platform mechanism is already generic |

The platform ships the *mechanisms*; each tenant's pack \+ rule configuration expresses their specific obligations. New regulation → new rules, not new code.

---

## **10\. Escalation as a Compliance Feature**

The human-handover system (Core Engine doc §7) is also the compliance pressure valve, so it's worth restating from this angle: legal threats, payment disputes, harassment claims, or a request to speak to a human **always** route to a person — these triggers live in the always-on `escalation_policy` rule set that packs can extend but not remove. And once escalated, automated contact with that customer is locked until a human closes the loop. An AI that knows when to stop is the strongest compliance feature of all.

# Deployment & Testing Strategy

# **Deployment & Testing Strategy**

---

## **1\. What This Document Covers**

Two questions every serious project must answer before writing much code:

1. **How does this run?** — environments, servers, deployment process, monitoring, and what we do when something breaks at 2 AM.  
2. **How do we know it works?** — and for an AI agent, "works" means more than passing unit tests: it means the agent *behaves correctly in conversation*, which needs its own kind of testing.

---

## **2\. Environments**

| Environment | Where | Purpose | Telephony |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Local** | Each developer's machine (Docker Compose) | Development. Full stack runs locally except real calls | Simulated calls (see §7.3) |
| **Staging** | Small Azure VM | Pre-release testing, client demos | Real provider account with test numbers — real calls to team phones |
| **Production** | Azure VM(s), same region as telephony provider's India endpoints | Live | Real |

Rule one: **staging is identical to production in shape** — same Docker images, same compose layout, smaller machine. Anything that only exists in production is a bug waiting for its moment.

Rule two: staging uses a separate database and separate provider accounts. No shared anything.

---

## **3\. Production Deployment Layout**

Everything is containerized and orchestrated with **Docker Compose** (your current PM2-on-VM approach works for Node-style processes, but here we have Python services, workers, Redis, and Postgres with exact version needs — containers keep all of it reproducible; and it's one `docker compose up -d` instead of a hand-configured VM).

Azure Ubuntu VM (production)  
├── caddy                    \# reverse proxy \+ automatic HTTPS  
├── core-api        ×2       \# the Core Platform (two replicas)  
├── voice-service   ×2       \# the Voice Session Service  
├── worker          ×2       \# Celery workers (post-call, campaigns, retries)  
├── beat            ×1       \# the scheduler (reminders, retention jobs)  
├── dashboard                \# React build, served as static files by caddy  
├── postgres:16              \# with pgvector; nightly encrypted backups → Azure Blob  
└── redis:7                  \# persistence on (AOF)

**Sizing to start:** one `Standard_D4s` (4 vCPU / 16 GB) carries the whole stack comfortably at launch scale (tens of concurrent calls). The first scaling move, when needed, is not Kubernetes — it's: move Postgres to Azure's managed Flexible Server, and put the voice service on its own VM (it's the component whose load grows with concurrent calls). That two-step gets you to hundreds of concurrent calls before any orchestration complexity is justified.

**Configuration & secrets:** all config via environment variables (pydantic-settings); secrets pulled from **Azure Key Vault** at container start — never stored in the repo, images, or a `.env` on the server.

**Database migrations:** Alembic, run as an explicit deploy step (not on container boot). Migrations must be backward-compatible one version back (add column → deploy code → later remove old column), so a code rollback never requires a database rollback.

---

## **4\. CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions)**

Every push to a pull request runs, in order:

1. **Lint \+ type check** (ruff, mypy) — cheap failures first  
2. **Unit tests** — fast, no external services  
3. **Integration tests** — against real Postgres \+ Redis spun up in the pipeline  
4. **Engine behavior suite** — the conversation tests from §7.2 (the ones that don't need paid LLM calls run on every PR; the full suite runs nightly)  
5. **Build images** — tagged with the git SHA

Merge to `main` → auto-deploy to **staging**. Production deploys are **manual approval** (one click, but a human clicks it), deploying the exact staging-verified image by SHA — we never rebuild for production.

**Rollback** is redeploying the previous SHA: one command, under two minutes. Every deploy is recorded (who, what SHA, when) in the audit events.

---

## **5\. Monitoring — Knowing It's Healthy**

Three layers, from cheap to deep:

**1\. Is it up?** `GET /health/deep` checked every 30 s by an external uptime monitor (the VM cannot monitor itself). Checks DB, Redis, and each provider's reachability.

**2\. Is it performing?** Prometheus \+ Grafana dashboards on the numbers that matter:

* Per-stage turn latency (p50/p95) — the §5 voice budget, live  
* Concurrent calls, call setup failures, provider error rates and circuit-breaker state  
* Queue depths (a growing Celery queue means the post-call pipeline is falling behind)  
* LLM token spend per hour (cost surprises show up here first)

**3\. Is it behaving?** The agent-quality numbers, computed from decision traces:

* Escalation rate, blocked-action rate, average confidence  
* Hallucination flags (grounding checks that failed in step 11\)  
* Conversation outcomes distribution

**Alerts that page a human** (kept deliberately short so alerts stay meaningful): API down · p95 turn latency \> 2.5 s for 5 min · provider circuit breaker open · queue depth beyond threshold · disk \> 85% · **any hallucination flag** (rare enough to investigate individually) · error rate spike.

**Logs:** structured JSON (structlog), PII-masked at the logger (Compliance doc §5), shipped to one place, searchable by `request_id`/`trace_id` — the same IDs the API returns in errors, so a bug report can be traced end to end in minutes.

---

## **6\. Cost Watch (worth its own section)**

Voice AI has a per-minute marginal cost (telephony \+ STT \+ TTS \+ LLM ≈ ₹4–9/min depending on providers and call complexity). Two protections from day one:

* A **per-tenant daily budget** in config; crossing 80% alerts, crossing 100% pauses outbound campaigns (inbound and service calls continue).  
* The cost per call is computed and stored on each call record — so "which campaign / which conversation type is expensive" is a dashboard query, not a spreadsheet archaeology project at month-end.

---

## **7\. Testing Strategy**

The pyramid, from bottom (many, fast, cheap) to top (few, slow, real):

### **7.1 Unit & integration tests (the classical base)**

Unit tests for all deterministic logic — and note that our safety-critical code is *deliberately* deterministic, which makes it thoroughly unit-testable: rule evaluation, tool validation checks, slot computation, state transitions, confidence banding, PII masking. Target: this layer alone catches any regression in the safety machinery.

Integration tests against real Postgres/Redis for: repositories with tenant isolation (including proving that tenant A queries can't see tenant B rows), the booking transaction under concurrent access (two simultaneous bookings of the last slot — exactly one must win), migration up/down, webhook signature verification.

### **7.2 Engine behavior tests (the layer specific to AI agents)**

This is where an agent project lives or dies. We maintain a **conversation test suite**: scripted dialogues with assertions, run against the real engine with either a mocked LLM (deterministic, every PR) or the real LLM (nightly \+ pre-release).

\# tests/conversations/booking\_happy\_path.yaml  
setup:  
  customer: { state: interested, facts: \[{ category: preference, key: preferred\_time, value: morning }\] }  
  scheduling: { centre: vapi\_main, free\_slots: \["2026-07-18T10:30", "2026-07-18T11:30"\] }  
turns:  
  \- user: "I'd like to come in this Saturday"  
    expect:  
      action\_in: \[respond, confirm\]  
      must\_mention\_only\_slots\_from: scheduling.free\_slots   \# anti-hallucination assertion  
  \- user: "10:30 works"  
    expect: { action: confirm }                             \# requires\_confirmation gate  
  \- user: "yes, confirm it"  
    expect:  
      tool\_executed: book\_appointment  
      state\_changed\_to: appointment\_booked

The suite covers, at minimum: every tool's happy path · every `failure_policy` branch (slot taken, system error) · every rule (DNC mid-call, calling hours, identity verification demanded) · confidence behavior (garbled input → clarify, not act) · escalation triggers (angry VIP, legal keywords) · the interrupting states (call-later then resume) · and **adversarial turns**: the customer asks for a discount that doesn't exist, claims a booking that doesn't exist, tries to change someone else's appointment. Every incident found in production later becomes a new test here permanently — the suite only grows.

**Rule tests specifically:** the `POST /rules/{name}/test` dry-run endpoint is also used in CI — each rule set ships with scenario fixtures asserting exactly which rules fire.

### **7.3 Voice pipeline tests**

* **Simulated calls:** a test harness plays recorded audio files (clean speech, noisy speech, interruptions, silence, Hinglish accents) through the full pipeline as if from the provider — runs in CI, no phone network needed. Asserts transcripts, barge-in stop time (\<150 ms), silence-prompt behavior, disclosure-before-recording ordering.  
* **Real-call tests (staging, scripted, manual):** a checklist of \~25 scenarios executed by the team on real phones over the real provider before every release: booking end-to-end, interrupting mid-pitch, going silent, saying "stop calling me", asking for a human, poor-network call from a mobile. Each scenario has pass criteria including subjective ones ("did the pause feel natural?") — voice quality cannot be fully asserted by machines.

### **7.4 Load testing**

Before launch and before any big campaign: synthetic concurrent calls (the simulated-call harness, parallelized) at **2× expected peak**, sustained 30 minutes. Pass criteria: p95 end-to-end turn latency \< 2 s · zero dropped sessions · zero double-bookings under concurrent slot pressure · queue depths recover after the wave.

### **7.5 The golden set (regression protection for the AI's judgment)**

\~100 real (anonymized) conversation turns with human-approved expected behavior, re-run against the engine whenever anything that shapes decisions changes: prompts, models, provider swap, retrieval tuning. The diff report — "the new prompt changed the agent's action on 4 of 100 goldens, here they are" — is reviewed by a human before activation. This is what makes "let's improve the prompt" safe instead of a gamble.

---

## **8\. Release Process**

1. Feature merged → auto-deployed to staging  
2. CI green including nightly engine suite with real LLM  
3. Real-call checklist on staging (§7.3) — for releases touching voice  
4. Golden-set diff reviewed — for releases touching prompts/models/retrieval  
5. Manual approve → production deploy (same image SHA)  
6. **Canary window:** first 30 minutes watched live on the dashboard; one command rolls back  
7. Config changes (rules, prompts, packs) don't need deploys at all — they're versioned rows with one-click rollback (their own release process is: edit → dry-run test → activate → watch)

---

## **9\. Go-Live Checklist (per tenant)**

Infrastructure ready is not launch ready. Before a tenant's number goes live:

* \[ \] Industry pack loaded; rules dry-run tested against scenario fixtures  
* \[ \] Knowledge base uploaded; retrieval spot-checked with `POST /knowledge/search` on the 20 most likely customer questions  
* \[ \] DNC registry imported; calling-hours rules match the tenant's region  
* \[ \] Disclosure script legally reviewed by the tenant  
* \[ \] Escalation path staffed — a real human answers the transfer number during calling hours (test it)  
* \[ \] Provider numbers verified, webhook signatures confirmed, budgets and alerts configured  
* \[ \] Real-call checklist executed on the tenant's own configuration  
* \[ \] The tenant has dashboard access and knows how to: pause everything (one button), read a decision trace, and edit a rule  
* \[ \] First campaign starts small: 50 calls, human reviews outcomes and a sample of traces, then scale

---

## **10\. When Things Break — the Short Runbook**

| Symptom | First response |
| ----- | ----- |
| Latency alert | Grafana → which stage grew? Provider stage → check circuit breaker/fallback. Brain stage → check LLM provider status \+ token queue |
| Calls failing to connect | Provider dashboard \+ webhook log; verify signature failures aren't rejecting events |
| Queue depth climbing | Scale workers (`docker compose up -d --scale worker=4`); investigate the slow task after |
| Hallucination flag | Pull the trace, find which grounding check failed, add the case to the conversation suite, fix, redeploy |
| Bad rule activated | One-click rollback to previous version in the dashboard — no deploy |
| Full outage | Redeploy previous SHA; if data-related, restore drill procedure (practiced monthly, §8 of Compliance doc) |

Every incident ends with a new test in the suite. That's the loop that makes the system *more* reliable every time it fails.
